bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- US market and tariff concentration — Over 59% of the Company's exports are distributed in the USA. The MD&A records that FY26 saw severe mid-year headwinds from the US reciprocal tariff regime, which temporarily squeezed traditional Western market channels. Relief depends on the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement, which is described only as an active dialogue in progress and has not been concluded.
- Geographic concentration of the export base — Beyond the 59% USA share, Europe and the UK contribute 18% of exports and the rest of the world (GCC ME/MENA, Far East, ANZ) up to 10%, with India at 13% of revenue share. Demand is therefore concentrated in a small number of developed retail markets whose inventory and consumption cycles move together.
- Dependence on trade agreements that are not yet fully operative — Much of the stated growth runway rests on duty relief that is still pending. The India-EU FTA is at the negotiation stage with proposals indicating duty-free access on 99-99.5% of Indian exports; the India-UK CETA becomes effective only from 15 July 2026; the India-US BTA is under negotiation. Delay or dilution would leave in place the 10-12% tariffs historically applied to home textile exports.
- Demand volatility and retailer inventory corrections — Management states that FY26 financial performance was moderated by transient headwinds including global inventory corrections, elevated tariffs and demand volatility. Home textiles is a discretionary, replacement-cycle category, so destocking by major international retail chains transmits quickly into order volumes and pricing.
- Cotton raw-material price exposure — Cotton is described as essential to the business and the MD&A tracks the cotton economy as a macroeconomic factor. Input-cost movements pass through directly into a cotton-intensive manufacturing base, and management's earlier commentary attributes stabilised industry margins specifically to predictable raw-material procurement costs.
- Foreign-exchange dependence of export realisations — The MD&A attributes part of FY26 export competitiveness to fluctuations in the INR/USD and INR/EUR currency corridors optimising net export realisations. A tailwind described in these terms is symmetrical: rupee appreciation would compress realisations for an export-led manufacturer with 60%-plus of sales in a single foreign currency.
- Competitive pressure from duty-advantaged sourcing origins — The MD&A notes India can 'finally match the Duty-free status enjoyed by Pakistan and Bangladesh' only once the UK FTA takes effect, and that near-shoring hubs such as Turkey and Mexico compete on speed-to-market. Until logistics and duty parity are realised, competing origins retain a structural cost and lead-time advantage in key markets.
- Exposure to global supply-chain and trade-route disruption — The outlook flags that the global environment remains subject to fragmentation, with supply-chain disruption from conflict in the Middle East. The Company's route to market depends on long ocean corridors, so disruption to West Asian trade routes affects both freight cost and delivery reliability for an export-oriented manufacturer.

outlook.body: Welspun Living's FY26 expansion story is centred on nearshore US pillow manufacturing and on the emerging flooring and advanced-textiles verticals. The year marked the commencement of commercial production at the greenfield pillow facility in Nevada, USA - described in the corporate-overview timeline as 'Launched another pillow manufacturing unit in Nevada, USA, expanding its global manufacturing footprint' - which follows the fully automated Ohio pillow plant set up in 2024. Management states that growth in the pillows segment accelerated, supported by higher utilisation at the Ohio facility and the commencement of operations at Nevada, and frames the US pillow investment as a strategic entry into one of the fastest-growing home textile categories and a platform built closer to the consumer, not merely a tariff response; scaling US manufacturing in pillows and adjacent categories is named as an FY27 priority. The earlier build-out of the emerging businesses remains the other axis: the flooring manufacturing facility at Hyderabad (2020) and the Welspun Advanced Material facility in Telangana (commissioned 2023) for value-added technical textiles. Under BRSR Section A the Indian footprint is four manufacturing plants (Anjar, Vapi Textiles, Vapi Rugs and Hyderabad) plus one corporate office, with one international plant and five international offices. On the geographic side the Company is strengthening presence across the UK, Europe, Middle East, ANZ and Japan. The annual report does not state a rupee capex quantum: the capital-commitments note supplied as a named disclosure carries only its heading and column labels, with no readable figure, and BRSR Principle 2 reports no capex investment attributed to environmental and social improvement technologies in either FY26 or FY25 (R&D investment for that purpose is reported separately).

outlook.body:
- India is strengthening its position as a preferred sourcing destination, supported by evolving trade frameworks with the US, UK, EU, Japan and Australia, creating significant long-term opportunities for the textile sector.
- The India-UK CETA, effective 15 July 2026, grants duty-free access to 99% of Indian exports to the UK including home textiles, eliminating the 10-12% tariffs that previously applied; the EU and UK combined represent a home textile market worth over $30 billion.
- The India-EU FTA framework is designed to provide zero-duty access on 99-99.5% of Indian exports, opening the sustainability-driven European market where recycled polyester and organic cotton home textiles command 15-20% higher margins.
- Global supply-chain diversification and 'China+1' sourcing continue to shift volumes toward trusted manufacturing hubs with scale, reliability and compliance.
- The domestic consumer business is a key growth driver, with revenues growing about 9% year on year on stronger brand traction, premiumisation and channel diversification.
- The Indian domestic home textile market is shifting from unorganised commodities to a premium, brand-led ecosystem expanding at a 7.08% CAGR, propelled by a rising affluent middle class and compressed replacement cycles.
- Sustainability is becoming a key consideration in retailer sourcing decisions, so the Company's ESG leadership strengthens customer trust and differentiation.
- Rupee depreciation against major currencies has enhanced the price competitiveness of Indian exports, supporting export demand and potentially higher export volumes.
- Global cotton is expected to remain structurally sound and broadly stable, supported by gradual normalisation of trade flows and steady demand anchoring from the Indian and Chinese textile hubs.
- Management notes early signs of recovery: Q4 FY26 delivered healthy sequential revenue growth and improvements in EBITDA margins, and the Company enters FY27 with a strengthened balance sheet and improving market positioning.
- Near-term pressures from global inventory corrections, elevated tariffs and demand volatility are being progressively offset by India's evolving trade architecture and the realignment of global supply chains.
- The technical textiles opportunity: backed by India's largest spunlace capacity and Spunlace, Needlepunch and Thermal Bonding technologies, the Company is positioned to address rising demand for high-performance and sustainable non-woven solutions.

risks.note: Over 59% of the Company's exports are distributed in the USA. The MD&A records that FY26 saw severe mid-year headwinds from the US reciprocal tariff regime, which temporarily squeezed traditional Western market channels. Relief depends on the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement, which is described only as an active dialogue in progress and has not been concluded.

Beyond the 59% USA share, Europe and the UK contribute 18% of exports and the rest of the world (GCC ME/MENA, Far East, ANZ) up to 10%, with India at 13% of revenue share. Demand is therefore concentrated in a small number of developed retail markets whose inventory and consumption cycles move together.
risks.risk: Geographic concentration of the export base

risks.note: Much of the stated growth runway rests on duty relief that is still pending. The India-EU FTA is at the negotiation stage with proposals indicating duty-free access on 99-99.5% of Indian exports; the India-UK CETA becomes effective only from 15 July 2026; the India-US BTA is under negotiation. Delay or dilution would leave in place the 10-12% tariffs historically applied to home textile exports.
risks.risk: Dependence on trade agreements that are not yet fully operative

risks.note: Management states that FY26 financial performance was moderated by transient headwinds including global inventory corrections, elevated tariffs and demand volatility. Home textiles is a discretionary, replacement-cycle category, so destocking by major international retail chains transmits quickly into order volumes and pricing.
risks.risk: Demand volatility and retailer inventory corrections

risks.note: Cotton is described as essential to the business and the MD&A tracks the cotton economy as a macroeconomic factor. Input-cost movements pass through directly into a cotton-intensive manufacturing base, and management's earlier commentary attributes stabilised industry margins specifically to predictable raw-material procurement costs.

The MD&A attributes part of FY26 export competitiveness to fluctuations in the INR/USD and INR/EUR currency corridors optimising net export realisations. A tailwind described in these terms is symmetrical: rupee appreciation would compress realisations for an export-led manufacturer with 60%-plus of sales in a single foreign currency.

The MD&A notes India can 'finally match the Duty-free status enjoyed by Pakistan and Bangladesh' only once the UK FTA takes effect, and that near-shoring hubs such as Turkey and Mexico compete on speed-to-market. Until logistics and duty parity are realised, competing origins retain a structural cost and lead-time advantage in key markets.
risks.risk: Competitive pressure from duty-advantaged sourcing origins

risks.note: The outlook flags that the global environment remains subject to fragmentation, with supply-chain disruption from conflict in the Middle East. The Company's route to market depends on long ocean corridors, so disruption to West Asian trade routes affects both freight cost and delivery reliability for an export-oriented manufacturer.
risks.risk: Exposure to global supply-chain and trade-route disruption

currentContext.strengths: Global leadership in home textile exports combined with a domestic retail presence; India's largest exporter of home textiles and the leading supplier to the US market for over 36 years|Vertically integrated operations with a robust sourcing and manufacturing ecosystem, giving operational agility and supply-chain resilience|Nearshore US manufacturing through the Ohio and Nevada pillow facilities, placing capacity inside the largest end market|Innovation moat of 50 global patents and proprietary technologies such as HygroCotton, GX Pillow and Wel-Trak; innovation-led products contributed approximately 22% of revenue in FY26|ESG differentiation: ranked #1 globally in the 2025 S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment for the Textile, Apparel & Luxury Goods category, with the CSA score rising from 59 in FY23 to 90 in FY26|Multi-brand portfolio spanning premium, luxury, institutional and mass segments (Christy, Welhome, Welspun, SPACES) with shelf presence across leading global retailers|India's largest spunlace capacity, with Spunlace, Needlepunch and Thermal Bonding technologies in advanced textiles|Decades-long retailer relationships that the Company chose to protect through the FY26 US tariff escalation, at a short-term cost, to preserve trust and market position
currentContext.strategies: Deepen the branded and consumer businesses, building towards the stated ambition of becoming the 'FMCG of textiles' where brands, innovation and consumer relationships create value alongside manufacturing scale.|Capitalise on the opportunities emerging from new trade agreements, specifically the India-UK CETA effective 15 July 2026, the advanced India-EU FTA and the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement.|Scale the US manufacturing presence in pillows and adjacent categories, treating nearshore capacity as a strategic entry into one of the fastest-growing home textile categories rather than only a tariff response.|Continue geographic diversification to reduce US concentration; the non-US revenue contribution expanded to about 41% in FY26.|Continue investing in innovation, technology and design to strengthen differentiation, backed by 50 global patents and proprietary technologies such as HygroCotton, GX Pillow and Wel-Trak.|Advance the Welspun 2.0 framework built on six value drivers - growth drivers (regional expansion, brands and emerging businesses) and value enablers (innovation, digitisation and ESG).|Strengthen regional presence in the UK, Europe, Middle East, ANZ and Japan to deepen customer relationships and diversify market exposure.|Grow the emerging businesses in flooring and advanced textiles as new avenues of growth into high-potential, value-added segments.|Maintain financial discipline - cash generation, working-capital and inventory optimisation, receivables management and prudent capital allocation - to preserve balance sheet strength as a strategic advantage.|Use sustainability leadership as a competitive moat in retailer sourcing decisions, having ranked #1 globally in the 2025 S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment for Textiles, Apparel & Luxury Goods.
currentContext.expansion: Welspun Living's FY26 expansion story is centred on nearshore US pillow manufacturing and on the emerging flooring and advanced-textiles verticals. The year marked the commencement of commercial production at the greenfield pillow facility in Nevada, USA - described in the corporate-overview timeline as 'Launched another pillow manufacturing unit in Nevada, USA, expanding its global manufacturing footprint' - which follows the fully automated Ohio pillow plant set up in 2024. Management states that growth in the pillows segment accelerated, supported by higher utilisation at the Ohio facility and the commencement of operations at Nevada, and frames the US pillow investment as a strategic entry into one of the fastest-growing home textile categories and a platform built closer to the consumer, not merely a tariff response; scaling US manufacturing in pillows and adjacent categories is named as an FY27 priority. The earlier build-out of the emerging businesses remains the other axis: the flooring manufacturing facility at Hyderabad (2020) and the Welspun Advanced Material facility in Telangana (commissioned 2023) for value-added technical textiles. Under BRSR Section A the Indian footprint is four manufacturing plants (Anjar, Vapi Textiles, Vapi Rugs and Hyderabad) plus one corporate office, with one international plant and five international offices. On the geographic side the Company is strengthening presence across the UK, Europe, Middle East, ANZ and Japan. The annual report does not state a rupee capex quantum: the capital-commitments note supplied as a named disclosure carries only its heading and column labels, with no readable figure, and BRSR Principle 2 reports no capex investment attributed to environmental and social improvement technologies in either FY26 or FY25 (R&D investment for that purpose is reported separately).
currentContext.mdna: India is strengthening its position as a preferred sourcing destination, supported by evolving trade frameworks with the US, UK, EU, Japan and Australia, creating significant long-term opportunities for the textile sector.|The India-UK CETA, effective 15 July 2026, grants duty-free access to 99% of Indian exports to the UK including home textiles, eliminating the 10-12% exports, opening the sustainability-driven European market where recycled polyester and organic cotton home textiles command 15-20% higher margins.|Global supply-chain diversification and 'China+1' sourcing continue to shift volumes toward trusted manufacturing hubs with scale, reliability and compliance.|The domestic consumer business is a key growth driver, with revenues growing about 9% year on year on stronger brand traction, premiumisation and channel diversification.|The Indian domestic home textile market is shifting from unorganised commodities to a premium, brand-led ecosystem expanding at a 7.08% CAGR, propelled by a rising affluent middle class and compressed replacement cycles.|Sustainability is becoming a key consideration in retailer sourcing decisions, so the Company's ESG leadership strengthens customer trust and differentiation.|Rupee depreciation against major currencies has enhanced the price competitiveness of Indian exports, supporting export demand risks.note: Over 59% of the Company's exports are distributed in the USA. The MD&A records that FY26 saw severe mid-year headwinds from the US reciprocal tariff regime, which temporarily squeezed traditional Western market channels. Relief depends on the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement, which is described only as an active dialogue in progress and has not been concluded.

risks.risk: Geographic concentration of the export base
risks.note: Beyond the 59% USA share, Europe and the UK contribute 18% of exports and the rest of the world (GCC ME/MENA, Far East, ANZ) up to 10%, with India at 13% of revenue share. Demand is therefore concentrated in a small number of developed retail markets whose inventory and consumption cycles move together.

risks.risk: Dependence on trade agreements that are not yet fully operative
risks.note: Much of the stated growth runway rests on duty relief that is still pending. The India-EU FTA is at the negotiation stage with proposals indicating duty-free access on 99-99.5% of Indian exports; the India-UK CETA becomes effective only from 15 July 2026; the India-US BTA is under negotiation. Delay or dilution would leave in place the 10-12% tariffs historically applied to home textile exports.

risks.risk: Demand volatility and retailer inventory corrections
risks.note: Management states that FY26 financial performance was moderated by transient headwinds including global inventory corrections, elevated tariffs and demand volatility. Home textiles is a discretionary, replacement-cycle category, so destocking by major international retail chains transmits quickly into order volumes and pricing.

Cotton is described as essential to the business and the MD&A tracks the cotton economy as a macroeconomic factor. Input-cost movements pass through directly into a cotton-intensive manufacturing base, and management's earlier commentary attributes stabilised industry margins specifically to predictable raw-material procurement costs.

The MD&A attributes part of FY26 export competitiveness to fluctuations in the INR/USD and INR/EUR currency corridors optimising net export realisations. A tailwind described in these terms is symmetrical: rupee appreciation would compress realisations for an export-led manufacturer with 60%-plus of sales in a single foreign currency.

risks.risk: Competitive pressure from duty-advantaged sourcing origins
risks.note: The MD&A notes India can 'finally match the Duty-free status enjoyed by Pakistan and Bangladesh' only once the UK FTA takes effect, and that near-shoring hubs such as Turkey and Mexico compete on speed-to-market. Until logistics and duty parity are realised, competing origins retain a structural cost and lead-time advantage in key markets.

risks.risk: Exposure to global supply-chain and trade-route disruption
risks.note: The outlook flags that the global environment remains subject to fragmentation, with supply-chain disruption from conflict in the Middle East. The Company's route to market depends on long ocean corridors, so disruption to West Asian trade routes affects both freight cost and delivery reliability for an export-oriented manufacturer.

thesis (one line): FY26 was an "external-shock-absorption" year (revenue -11.5% YoY on US tariff/demand softness) — but Q4 marked a decisive sequential inflection (rev +7.7% QoQ, EBITDA margin 10.8% +313bps), with management guiding FY27 to double-digit topline growth and "teens" EBITDA margin, led by tariff easing, multi-year FTA tailwinds, branded/domestic scale-up and a sharply deleveraged balance sheet (net debt -52% YoY).

|---|---|---|---|

| **Cash conversion cycle** | 82 days | improved | Stronger operating control |

**CALL-OUTS:**
- **US tariff:** Trajectory Mar (10%) → 25% → 50% (28-Aug) → back to ~10% (Feb), now BTA discussions at 15–18%. ~10% applies till ~late Jul-2026 (Section 122 till June-end). Section 301 also initiated on India (risk). >80% of business is **FOB** → tariff handled directly with customers; sharing on a **"50:50"** basis. Mgmt: zero customer loss through cycle.
- **Cotton/RM:** Cotton +10%, man-made fibers +20%, yarn (terry/bedsheet) +20–30%, dyes & chemicals +20%, crude +40%. Cost inflation is broad, not just cotton. Cotton inventory cover **until October**.
- **Forex:** INR at ~96/USD; mgmt says **no net-delta gain** from depreciation — offset by RM inflation; hedge policy unchanged (group-level 65/35 maintained across Welspun world).
guidance (critical):
- **Revenue:** FY27 targeting **double-digit topline growth**; exit FY27 on stronger trajectory. India market to grow **~26–30%**.
- **Margin:** FY27 EBITDA margin **"advancing into the teens"** (low-teens). Path back to 14–15% deferred — no firm timeline given (vs 9.1% FY26 / 13.6% FY25).
- **Medium-term aspiration:** **INR 15,000 cr revenue in ~3 years**; current optimized capacity can support **INR 11,500–12,000 cr**.
- **Mix / segment targets:** Domestic to **INR 1,000 cr** ("spot on"); Flooring to **INR 1,000 cr** (soft-flooring led); branded business ~19% of revenue (rising); innovation 22% of business.
- **US pillows:** FY26 ~USD 27.5m → **double to ~USD 60m in FY27** (Ohio + Nevada). Nevada (4.5m pcs, USD 13m capex) partial commercial production from 31-Mar-2026; Ohio at 60% utilization.
- **Capex:** FY26 INR 472 cr; **FY27 INR 400–500 cr** (modernization, automation, debottlenecking — not greenfield-heavy).
- **Utilization:** Core (towels/sheets/bath rugs) at **86%+**, expected to rise.
- **Balance sheet:** Targeting **net-debt-zero in FY27**.
- **ROCE:** To improve to **>15%**, "asset-light" growth right now.
- **Capital return:** Buyback approved at **INR 175/share, up to INR 252 cr** (funded from cash); dividend recommended at 10% per equity share.
demand / pipeline:
- Q4 US retail demand "still very robust" despite inflation; mgmt sees growth vs LY even with US inflation. No meaningful adverse change in large-retailer ordering behavior over last 2–3 months despite tariff uncertainty.
- Restocking question (Shweta Sharma): mgmt did not confirm explicit restocking; framed FY27 as "reasonable growth" + double-digit globally.
- Non-US share expanded to **41%** (Europe, UK, India, ROW) — key diversification lever.
- FTAs as multi-year demand unlock: UK by June-end (Q2 FY27 visibility), EU by Jan-end, plus Japan/Australia. EU+UK = USD 30bn+ home-textile market.
- India sourcing share (OTEXA): 45% cotton terry towels, 60% cotton sheets.
segment detail:
- **Home textile (core, towels/sheets):** FY26 -11.2%; utilization recovering to 86%+; leaders in bath, present in 50+ countries; pillows/utility & fashion bedding "high potential."
- **Pillows / sleep solutions:** Ohio at 60% util, doubled to USD 27.5m (from USD 15m FY25); Nevada commissioned 31-Mar-2026 (man-made + natural fiber filling, UVR upside). Sleep positioned as "as big a category as towels."
- **Global Flooring:** FY26 -25.1% (worst-hit by West Asia logistics + US tariff). Soft flooring recovering (20%+ margin potential, CAGR growth) via US co-branded carpet-tile collections + ANZ diversification. Hard flooring being **rationalized** to protect margins.
- **Domestic Flooring:** +18% FY26; housing/hospitality/institutional; architect/designer specification-led demand.
- **Advanced Textiles:** FY26 -20% to INR 452 cr; shifting from commoditized to value-added (sustainable diapers, fem-care, specialty wipes, protective apparel, jacket insulation). Target EBITDA steady-state **~20%+**; focus Hometech/Medtech/Protech/Indoortech.
- **Branded:** Branded portfolio 19.3% of FY26 revenue; global brands 12%. Christy +15% (UK strength, US e-comm); Welhome USD 19.4m (N. America + Japan/UK/China/Taiwan expansion). Domestic Welspun +44% / Spaces +19% YoY in Q4.
growth / optionality:
- **Domestic branded D2C:** India "inflection point"; Welspun +44%, Spaces +19% (Q4); quick-commerce + e-commerce + offline (modern/general/regional trade, mom-and-pop); D2C exposure being built. Target INR 1,000 cr.
- **Flooring scale-up:** Soft flooring + domestic flooring to INR 1,000 cr; FTA-enabled UK/Europe/ME/ANZ commercial & hospitality penetration.
- **Advanced textiles:** UK/EU FTAs strengthen access for technical textiles, non-wovens, wipes (ESG/compliance moat); value-added shift.
- **China+1 / India sourcing:** India share gains (45% towels, 60% sheets per OTEXA); FTAs (UK/EU/Japan/Australia) structurally enhance competitiveness.
- **US nearshore manufacturing:** Ohio + Nevada pillow plants; partnerships in US & Canada (retail + hospitality).
- **Institutional/hospitality B2B:** Welspun Hospitality with Hyatt, IHG, Wyndham, Marriott; religious tourism (~20% growth) tailwind in India.
- **M&A:** Open-ended; would focus on own-brands / geographic expansion.
margins & cost:
- Q4 EBITDA 10.8% (+313bps QoQ) on utilization, mix, cost rationalization, favorable forex.
- FY26 9.1% (vs 13.6% LY) — volume + tariff realization drag.
- **Cotton +10%; MMF +20%; yarn +20–30%; dyes/chem +20%; crude +40%** — broad RM inflation. Pricing power via customer "50:50" cost-sharing conversations; weak demand limits full pass-through.
- Forex INR 96 — no net-delta gain (offset by RM). Hedge 65/35 group policy unchanged.
- Cost governance/controls cited as structural margin lever for FY27.
capex:
- FY26 total capex INR 472 cr (productivity, sustainability, selective growth).
- FY27 capex **INR 400–500 cr** — modernization, automation, debottlenecking.
- Nevada pillow plant: USD 13m, 4.5m pcs, partial commercial production 31-Mar-2026.
capital allocation:
- **Buyback** at INR 175/share, up to **INR 252 cr** (from cash).
- **Dividend** 10% per equity share (subject to approval).
- Net debt INR 775 cr (-52% YoY); FCF INR 956 cr (+8.5x); targeting **net-debt-zero FY27**.
- ROCE to improve to >15%, asset-light approach.
risks:
- **US demand/tariff:** Section 122 expiry (June-end), Section 301 on India unresolved; BTA outcome (15% vs 18%) pending; tariff-refund uncertain (>80% FOB, customer-dependent). US inflation a watch-item.
- **Customer concentration / B2B:** Global B2B & others = ~52% of business (~INR 4,400 cr), -12% YoY — concentrated US exposure (mgmt insists no customer loss, demand-driven decline).
- **RM inflation:** Broad cotton/MMF/crude/chemicals spike; cotton cover only to October.
- **West Asia geopolitics:** Flooring most vulnerable; Strait of Hormuz/Red Sea (GCC ~2% of rev, FOB; Cape of Good Hope reroute adds 15–20 days).
- **FX:** INR 96, no net gain; demand softness limits pricing power.
- **Hard flooring:** Structurally weak, being rationalized.
mgmt tone: Confident and reassuring — "Q4 was about stabilization; FY27 about scaling profitably." Repeatedly emphasized zero customer loss, balance-sheet de-risking, FTA optionality and branded/domestic momentum. Notably evasive on precise FY27 margin recovery to 14–15% (deferred to "teens"), and gave no clean PAT figure. Heavy reliance on "50:50 cost-sharing" framing to deflect RM/tariff pass-through concerns.
non-obvious takeaways:
- Non-US share now 41% — diversification thesis materially advanced; FTAs (UK Jun-end, EU Jan-end) are the explicit near-term catalysts.
- Pillows/sleep being positioned as a category "as big as towels" — US nearshore (Ohio/Nevada) doubling to USD 60m is the most concrete growth line.
- Buyback + dividend + net-debt-zero target simultaneously signals confidence and a capital-return pivot in a down year.
- Global B2B (52% of mix, -12%) is the silent overhang; recovery hinges entirely on US tariff/demand normalization.
- Advanced Textiles repositioning to 20%+ EBITDA value-added niches (fem-care, wipes, insulation) is an under-the-radar margin optionality.
- "Optimized capacity" supports only INR 11.5–12k cr vs INR 15k cr aspiration → implies future growth capex needed beyond FY27's maintenance-heavy spend.
challenges → beneficiaries:

|---|---|
| US tariff easing + India FTA (UK/EU/Japan/Australia) → India sourcing share gains (China+1) | Indian home-textile exporters broadly (Trident, Indo Count, Himatsingka) ✅ |
| Cotton/yarn/MMF/crude inflation | Upstream spinners / cotton yarn producers ⭐ |
| US nearshore pillow/sleep manufacturing | US-located filling/fiber suppliers |
| Domestic D2C + quick-commerce home-textile demand | Indian organized branded home-textile + Q-comm platforms |

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Welspun Living is India's largest exporter of home textiles and the leading supplier to the US market, with a vertically integrated bed, bath, rugs, advanced textiles and flooring portfolio sold across 60+ countries.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: The Company manufactures and markets home textiles (terry towels, bed sheets, top-of-bed, rugs and carpets, bath robes), advanced non-woven technical textiles (spunlace, needlepunch, wet wipes) and flooring solutions (carpet tiles, wall-to-wall carpet, area rugs, SPC tiles). It supplies leading global retailers on a B2B basis while building a direct consumer business through owned and licensed brands in India and internationally. Manufacturing hubs are at Anjar and Vapi in Gujarat and Telangana/Hyderabad in India, plus nearshore pillow plants in Ohio and Nevada in the US.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India is strengthening its position as a preferred sourcing destination, supported by evolving trade frameworks with the US, UK, EU, Japan and Australia, creating significant long-term opportunities for the textile sector.
- The India-UK CETA, effective 15 July 2026, grants duty-free access to 99% of Indian exports to the UK including home textiles, eliminating the 10-12% tariffs that previously applied; the EU and UK combined represent a home textile market worth over $30 billion.
- The India-EU FTA framework is designed to provide zero-duty access on 99-99.5% of Indian exports, opening the sustainability-driven European market where recycled polyester and organic cotton home textiles command 15-20% higher margins.
- Global supply-chain diversification and 'China+1' sourcing continue to shift volumes toward trusted manufacturing hubs with scale, reliability and compliance.
- The domestic consumer business is a key growth driver, with revenues growing about 9% year on year on stronger brand traction, premiumisation and channel diversification.
- The Indian domestic home textile market is shifting from unorganised commodities to a premium, brand-led ecosystem expanding at a 7.08% CAGR, propelled by a rising affluent middle class and compressed replacement cycles.
- Sustainability is becoming a key consideration in retailer sourcing decisions, so the Company's ESG leadership strengthens customer trust and differentiation.
- Rupee depreciation against major currencies has enhanced the price competitiveness of Indian exports, supporting export demand and potentially higher export volumes.
- Global cotton is expected to remain structurally sound and broadly stable, supported by gradual normalisation of trade flows and steady demand anchoring from the Indian and Chinese textile hubs.
- Management notes early signs of recovery: Q4 FY26 delivered healthy sequential revenue growth and improvements in EBITDA margins, and the Company enters FY27 with a strengthened balance sheet and improving market positioning.
- Near-term pressures from global inventory corrections, elevated tariffs and demand volatility are being progressively offset by India's evolving trade architecture and the realignment of global supply chains.
- The technical textiles opportunity: backed by India's largest spunlace capacity and Spunlace, Needlepunch and Thermal Bonding technologies, the Company is positioned to address rising demand for high-performance and sustainable non-woven solutions.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Welspun Living's FY26 expansion story is centred on nearshore US pillow manufacturing and on the emerging flooring and advanced-textiles verticals. The year marked the commencement of commercial production at the greenfield pillow facility in Nevada, USA - described in the corporate-overview timeline as 'Launched another pillow manufacturing unit in Nevada, USA, expanding its global manufacturing footprint' - which follows the fully automated Ohio pillow plant set up in 2024. Management states that growth in the pillows segment accelerated, supported by higher utilisation at the Ohio facility and the commencement of operations at Nevada, and frames the US pillow investment as a strategic entry into one of the fastest-growing home textile categories and a platform built closer to the consumer, not merely a tariff response; scaling US manufacturing in pillows and adjacent categories is named as an FY27 priority. The earlier build-out of the emerging businesses remains the other axis: the flooring manufacturing facility at Hyderabad (2020) and the Welspun Advanced Material facility in Telangana (commissioned 2023) for value-added technical textiles. Under BRSR Section A the Indian footprint is four manufacturing plants (Anjar, Vapi Textiles, Vapi Rugs and Hyderabad) plus one corporate office, with one international plant and five international offices. On the geographic side the Company is strengthening presence across the UK, Europe, Middle East, ANZ and Japan. The annual report does not state a rupee capex quantum: the capital-commitments note supplied as a named disclosure carries only its heading and column labels, with no readable figure, and BRSR Principle 2 reports no capex investment attributed to environmental and social improvement technologies in either FY26 or FY25 (R&D investment for that purpose is reported separately).
